sections.title: Prose scores do not scale
paragraphs: A human reviewer can read "pretty good, dock a point for tone" and move on. Automation cannot — it needs {{structuredOutput}} with fixed fields the pipeline can parse.
AiEval's {{judge}} returns JSON: an array of scores keyed by {{criterion}} id, plus optional notes. The automation phase reads that JSON and writes rows into Compare — no manual copy-paste.
When a {{judge}} replies with free-form paragraphs instead of JSON, scoring fails or fills partial blanks. That is a pipeline error, not a mysterious {{model}} quirk.
Good judge {{prompt}}s include the schema: field names, score ranges, and an example object. You are teaching the {{judge}} the wire format, not just the rubric prose.
Next: how to design judge output that parsers accept.
bullets: Scores keyed by {{criterion}} id, not display name alone.
Schema in the judge {{prompt}} reduces parse failures.

choices: The parser cannot extract criterion scores
check.explanation: Without {{structuredOutput}}, automation cannot map text to {{criterion}} rows — scoring stalls or records empty points.

sections.title: Schema and common failures
paragraphs: Minimal judge JSON includes a `scores` array: each entry has `criterionId`, `points`, and optional `notes`. Optional top-level `answerNotes` captures overall reasoning.
Failures you will see: markdown fences around JSON, trailing commas, wrong id strings, or numeric scores outside the rubric ladder. Parsers throw; humans fix the judge {{prompt}} or retry.
Click each output style to see whether automation can consume it. The optional Judge JSON lab lets you practice spotting parse-ready responses.
Anchors still matter: JSON with wrong semantics is valid syntax but bad judgment. Structure and rubric clarity work together.

reveals.reveal: Often fine — fences strip before parse, if the inner JSON is valid.
Not parseable — no {{structuredOutput}}; automation needs JSON fields.

reveals.prompt: Judge output: JSON with criterionId "accuracy" but rubric id is "c1".
reveals.reveal: Syntax passes, semantics fail — score may default or miss the row.

aside.title: Try in AiEval
aside.body: Run automation, open Compare, and confirm each {{criterion}} row has points plus {{judge}} notes — evidence the {{structuredOutput}} parsed.

sections.title: From judges to retrieval
paragraphs: Structured judge output completes the scoring half of an {{evaluation}} harness. The next lessons shift to knowledge: storing facts outside the {{contextWindow}} and fetching them with {{retrieval}}.
Keep the habit: any automated step — generate, judge, or later retrieve — needs explicit input/output contracts. Ambiguity at boundaries becomes silent data loss.
Next up: Semantic memory — durable knowledge you search by meaning instead of pasting into every {{prompt}}.
bullets: Schema examples in judge {{prompt}}s prevent format drift.
Explicit contracts at every pipeline step.

check.prompt: In one short phrase: why do {{judge}}s need {{structuredOutput}}?
check.explanation: {{structuredOutput}} lets the harness map each {{criterion}} to points without human transcription.

recapQuestions.prompt: Valid JSON but wrong criterionId strings cause what symptom?
recapQuestions.explanation: Syntax success is not semantic success — ids must match the rubric the parser expects.

recapQuestions.prompt: A teammate wraps judge JSON in markdown fences. Is that always fatal?
recapQuestions.explanation: Many pipelines strip code fences before JSON parse — still better to ask the {{judge}} for raw JSON in production.
